lessons.title: Boot Sequence
lessons.summary: How this training ground works — reading panes, the workbench, checks, and your HUD.

exercises.title: First signal
hints: Keep a running total as you loop over xs.
After adding xs[i] to the total, the mean so far is total / (i + 1).
total = 0; out = []; for i, x in enumerate(xs): total += x; out.append(total / (i + 1))

lessons.title: The RL Problem
lessons.summary: Agents, environments, rewards, returns and discounting — the vocabulary everything else is built on.

exercises.title: Discounted return
hints: discounted_return: loop with k = 0, 1, 2… and add gamma**k * rewards[k].
returns_to_go: start with G = 0 after the final step and walk the list in reverse.
G = 0; out = []; for r in reversed(rewards): G = r + gamma * G; out.append(G) — then reverse out.

exercises.title: The agent loop
hints: Use a `while True:` loop and `break` once terminated or truncated is True.
Accumulate `total += reward` and `steps += 1` inside the loop.
random_policy can be `return random.randrange(5)`.

lessons.title: Multi-Armed Bandits
lessons.summary: Exploration vs exploitation in the simplest possible RL problem — action values, ε-greedy, optimism, UCB and gradient bandits.

exercises.title: An ε-greedy bandit agent
hints: `incremental_update` is literally one line. In `epsilon_greedy`, draw `rng.random()` once: if it is below ε, explore.
To break ties: `best = np.flatnonzero(Q == Q.max())` gives the indices of every maximal arm; `rng.choice(best)` picks one. In `update`, increment `self.N[a]` *before* computing `1 / self.N[a]`.
`update`: `self.N[a] += 1; step = self.alpha if self.alpha is not None else 1.0 / self.N[a]; self.Q[a] = incremental_update(self.Q[a], r, step)`. Remember to wrap returned arms in `int(...)`.

exercises.title: The 10-armed testbed
hints: Allocate `rewards = np.zeros((n_runs, n_steps))` and the same for `optimal`; one row per run. At the end, `.mean(axis=0)` averages over runs.

Inside the run loop: `a = agent.act(); optimal[i, t] = a == bandit.optimal_action; r = bandit.pull(a); agent.update(a, r); rewards[i, t] = r`. Record optimality *before* pulling — a nonstationary bandit changes its best arm after each pull.

`compare_epsilons`: `results[eps] = run_testbed(lambda s, e=eps: EpsilonGreedyAgent(10, epsilon=e, seed=s), n_runs=n_runs, n_steps=n_steps, seed=seed)`. The `e=eps` default argument freezes the loop variable inside the lambda.

exercises.title: Upper Confidence Bound
hints: Use `np.log` (natural log). Start with `scores = np.full(len(Q), np.inf)` and only compute the bound where `N > 0`, so you never divide by zero.
A boolean mask does it in one line: `tried = N > 0; scores[tried] = Q[tried] + c * np.sqrt(np.log(t) / N[tried])`. In the loop, `t` already starts at 1 — don't pass `t - 1` or ln 0 appears.
Loop body: `a = ucb_action(Q, N, t, c); r = bandit.pull(a); N[a] += 1; Q[a] += (r - Q[a]) / N[a]; rewards.append(r); optimal.append(a == bandit.optimal_action)`.

lessons.title: Markov Decision Processes
lessons.summary: The formal model behind RL — states, dynamics, policies, value functions and the Bellman equations.

exercises.title: One-step lookahead
hints: `env.P[s][a]` is a short list of tuples. Two nested loops are enough: over `a in range(env.n_actions)`, then `for prob, s2, r, done in env.P[s][a]`.

Accumulate `q[a] += prob * (r + gamma * V[s2])`, but replace the `gamma * V[s2]` part with 0 when `done` is True. Terminal states themselves only have self-loops with reward 0 and done=True, so their q is 0 automatically.
`q[a] += prob * (r + (0.0 if done else gamma * V[s2]))`; `q_table` is `np.array([q_from_v(env, V, s, gamma) for s in range(env.n_states)])`; `greedy_policy` is `np.argmax(Q, axis=1)`.

exercises.title: Solving the Bellman equation exactly
hints: Three nested loops: states `s`, actions `a`, and outcomes `(prob, s2, r, done)` in `env.P[s][a]`. The weight of an outcome under the policy is `policy[s, a] * prob`.

Every outcome adds `w * r` to `r_pi[s]`. Only outcomes with `done == False` add `w` to `P_pi[s, s2]`. Terminal and wall states only have `done=True` self-loops, so their rows stay zero and their value comes out 0.
`solve_v`: `P_pi, r_pi = policy_model(env, policy); return np.linalg.solve(np.eye(env.n_states) - gamma * P_pi, r_pi)`.

exercises.title: Optimal policies by brute force
hints: `decision_states(env)` gives the list of states that need an action. `itertools.product(range(env.n_actions), repeat=len(states))` yields every tuple of actions for them.
For each tuple: `actions = np.zeros(env.n_states, dtype=int); actions[states] = choice; v = solve_v(env, np.eye(env.n_actions)[actions], gamma)`. Keep it if `v.sum()` beats the best so far.
`is_optimal`: `return all(abs(V[s] - q_from_v(env, V, s, gamma).max()) <= tol for s in range(env.n_states))`.

lessons.title: Dynamic Programming
lessons.summary: Planning with a perfect model — policy evaluation, policy improvement, policy iteration, value iteration and GPI.

exercises.title: Iterative policy evaluation
hints: `expected_update` is the same double loop as `q_from_v`, except each outcome is weighted by `policy[s, a] * prob` and everything is summed into one number.

Structure: `for sweep in range(1, max_sweeps + 1): delta = 0.0; for s in range(env.n_states): v_new = expected_update(...); delta = max(delta, abs(v_new - V[s])); V[s] = v_new` and then `if delta < theta: break`.
Return `V, sweep`. Make sure `V` is a float array you are allowed to modify: `V = np.zeros(env.n_states) if V is None else np.array(V, dtype=float)`.

exercises.title: Policy iteration
hints: `policy_improvement`: loop over states; `q = q_from_v(env, V, s, gamma)`; `best = int(np.argmax(q))`; then `new[s, best] = 1.0`.
Tie rule: `old_a = int(np.argmax(old_policy[s]))`; `if q[old_a] >= q[best] - tol: best = old_a`. Without it, two equally good actions can alternate forever and the loop never sees a stable policy.

`policy_iteration` loop: `iterations += 1; V = policy_evaluation(env, policy, gamma, theta, V); new = policy_improvement(env, V, gamma, old_policy=policy); if np.array_equal(new, policy): return policy, V, iterations; policy = new`.

exercises.title: Value iteration on a slippery world
hints: Value iteration is policy evaluation with the average over π replaced by a max over actions. The loop skeleton is the same as in exercise 1.

`for _ in range(max_sweeps): delta = 0.0; for s in range(env.n_states): v_new = q_from_v(env, V, s, gamma).max(); delta = max(delta, abs(v_new - V[s])); V[s] = v_new` then `deltas.append(delta)` and `if delta < theta: break`.
Policy extraction after the loop: `for s in range(env.n_states): policy[s, np.argmax(q_from_v(env, V, s, gamma))] = 1.0`.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo Methods
lessons.summary: Learn values and policies from complete episodes of experience — no model required. Blackjack, ε-soft control and importance sampling.

exercises.title: First-visit Monte Carlo prediction
hints: Keep two dicts, `returns_sum` and `returns_count` (a `collections.defaultdict` is handy). The estimate is their ratio — you could also keep a running mean.

Before the backward pass, record the first index at which each state appears: `first = {}; for t, (s, _, _) in enumerate(episode): first.setdefault(s, t)`. In the backward pass, skip time t when `first_visit and first[s] != t`.

G = 0.0
for t in range(len(episode) - 1, -1, -1):
    s, _, r = episode[t]
    G = r + gamma * G
    if first_visit and first[s] != t: continue
    returns_sum[s] += G; returns_count[s] += 1

…and finally `return {s: returns_sum[s] / returns_count[s] for s in returns_count}`.

exercises.title: On-policy MC control on Blackjack
hints: There is no separate 'improvement' step: because every new episode acts ε-greedily on the *latest* Q, evaluation and improvement are interleaved — generalised policy iteration, one episode at a time.
Keep a second dict `N = {state: np.zeros(n_actions)}` of visit counts next to Q. Create both entries when you first see a state, *before* calling epsilon_greedy on it.

exercises.title: Ordinary vs weighted importance sampling
hints: Keep two running sums across episodes: `sum_wg` (Σ ρG) and `sum_w` (Σ ρ). Then both estimates are one division each.

Inside one episode: start `rho = 1.0, G = 0.0`; for each step t, `rho *= pi(a, s) / b(a, s)` and `G += gamma**t * r`. If π would never take the action, ρ becomes 0 and the episode contributes nothing to the numerator.

for k, ep in enumerate(episodes, start=1):
    rho, G = 1.0, 0.0
    for t, (s, a, r) in enumerate(ep):
        rho *= pi(a, s) / b(a, s); G += gamma**t * r
    sum_wg += rho * G; sum_w += rho
    ordinary.append(sum_wg / k)
    weighted.append(sum_wg / sum_w if sum_w > 0 else 0.0)

lessons.title: Temporal-Difference Learning
lessons.summary: Learn a guess from a guess — TD(0), SARSA, Q-learning, Expected SARSA and Double Q-learning, with the cliff as the proving ground.

exercises.title: TD(0) on the random walk
hints: The episode loop is the same as in every lesson so far: `s, _ = env.reset()`, then `s2, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(policy(s))`. The only new thing is the update you do right after each step.
Use your own `td_error`: `V[s] += alpha * td_error(r, V[s], V[s2], gamma, terminated)`. Then `s = s2` and continue unless the episode is over.

def td_error(r, v_s, v_next, gamma, terminated):
    target = r if terminated else r + gamma * v_next
    return target - v_s

and in td0: `if V is None: V = np.full(env.n_states, float(init))` before the episode loop; `return V` at the end.

exercises.title: SARSA on the cliff
hints: The name is the update: S, A, R, S', A'. You must pick A' *before* updating, use it in the target, and then actually take it on the next step — do not pick a fresh action at the top of the loop.

Skeleton:

s, _ = env.reset(); a = epsilon_greedy(Q, s, epsilon, rng); G = 0.0
while True:
    s2, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(a); G += r
    a2 = epsilon_greedy(Q, s2, epsilon, rng)
    ...

...then `sarsa_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, a2, alpha, gamma, terminated)`; `if terminated or truncated: break`; `s, a = s2, a2`. After the loop, `returns.append(G)`. sarsa_update itself: `target = r if terminated else r + gamma * Q[s2, a2]; delta = target - Q[s, a]; Q[s, a] += alpha * delta; return delta`.

exercises.title: Q-learning on the cliff
hints: The behaviour policy (how you pick the action you take) is still ε-greedy. Only the *target* changes: it assumes you will act greedily from S' onwards.
`np.max(Q[s2])` is the value of the best action in S'. If `terminated`, there is no S' to bootstrap from: `target = r`.

Loop body:

a = epsilon_greedy(Q, s, epsilon, rng)
s2, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(a)
G += r
q_learning_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, alpha, gamma, terminated)
if terminated or truncated: break
s = s2

exercises.title: Double Q-learning vs maximisation bias
hints: The bias comes from using the *same* noisy numbers to both choose the best action and estimate its value. Two independent tables break that link: one chooses, the other judges.
A clean trick: `A, B = (Q1, Q2) if update_first else (Q2, Q1)`, then write the update once in terms of A (updated, selects) and B (evaluates).

Episode loop:

s, _ = env.reset()
while True:
    a = epsilon_greedy(Q1[s] + Q2[s], epsilon, rng)
    if s == env.A: went_left.append(a == env.LEFT)
    s2, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(a)
    double_q_update(Q1, Q2, s, a, r, s2, alpha, gamma, terminated, rng.random() < 0.5)
    if terminated or truncated: break
    s = s2

lessons.title: n-step Bootstrapping & Planning
lessons.summary: The dial between TD and Monte Carlo (n-step returns, eligibility traces), then learned models and Dyna-Q — imagining experience to learn faster.

exercises.title: n-step TD prediction
hints: Initialise `T = float('inf')` and `t = 0`. Each iteration: if `t < T`, take a step and append to `states`/`rewards`, setting `T = t + 1` when the episode ends. Then compute τ and update if τ ≥ 0. Break when `τ == T − 1`; otherwise `t += 1`.

Indices are the whole difficulty. The rewards that follow time τ are R_τ+1 … R_min(τ+n, T), i.e. the slice `rewards[tau + 1 : min(tau + n, T) + 1]`. Bootstrap from `V[states[tau + n]]` only if `tau + n < T` — otherwise the window already reaches the end of the episode. (Once T is set it is an int, so `min` returns an int you can slice with.)

if tau >= 0:
    end = min(tau + n, T)
    boot = V[states[tau + n]] if tau + n < T else 0.0
    G = nstep_target(rewards[tau + 1:end + 1], gamma, boot)
    V[states[tau]] += alpha * (G - V[states[tau]])
if tau == T - 1: break
t += 1

exercises.title: TD(λ) with eligibility traces
hints: It is the TD(0) loop from lesson 6 with two extra lines: the trace bump before the update and the decay after. The update itself becomes a numpy vector operation over the whole `V`.

Order matters. Compute δ first (using the *old* V), then `e[s] += 1`, then `V += alpha * delta * e`, then `e *= gamma * lam`. Swap the bump and the update and the current state gets no credit for its own TD error.

while True:
    s2, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(policy(s))
    delta = r + (0.0 if terminated else gamma * V[s2]) - V[s]
    e[s] += 1.0
    V += alpha * delta * e
    e *= gamma * lam
    if terminated or truncated: break
    s = s2

exercises.title: Dyna-Q on a maze
hints: The maze only rewards reaching G (+1), so the first episode is a long random walk for everyone. Planning pays off from episode 2: the single rewarding transition gets replayed and its value propagates backwards through the remembered transitions.

The model of a deterministic env is just a lookup table: overwrite `model[(s, a)]` every time you take `a` in `s`. Planning uses the same `q_update` as direct RL — the only difference is where the transition comes from.

Inside the episode loop:

a = epsilon_greedy(Q, s, epsilon, rng)
s2, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(a); n += 1
q_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, terminated, alpha, gamma)
model[(s, a)] = (r, s2, terminated)
plan(Q, model, n_planning, rng, alpha, gamma)
if terminated or truncated: break
s = s2

lessons.title: Function Approximation
lessons.summary: Replace the table with a parameterised function — features, linear values, semi-gradient TD, tile coding, and the deadly triad.

exercises.title: Linear values: gradient MC & semi-gradient TD(0)
hints: For a linear function the gradient ∇v̂(s, w) is simply the feature vector x(s), so every update has the shape `w += alpha * error * x`.
gradient_mc_update: first build the list of returns backwards (G = r + gamma * G), then loop over zip(xs, returns) and apply the update.
td0_update: `target = r if terminated else r + gamma * v_hat(w, x_next)`; `delta = target - v_hat(w, x)`; `w += alpha * delta * x`; `return delta`.

exercises.title: Build a tile coder
hints: `scaled = (x - self.low) / (self.high - self.low) * self.tiles` — now 1 unit = 1 tile.
You can do all tilings at once: `coords = np.floor(scaled[None, :] + self.offsets).astype(int)` has shape (n_tilings, dims). Clip it with `np.clip(coords, 0, self.tiles)`.
`flat = np.ravel_multi_index(coords.T, self.shape)` then `return np.arange(self.n_tilings) * self.tiles_per_tiling + flat`.

exercises.title: Semi-gradient SARSA on Mountain Car
hints: q_values: fancy indexing `w[:, idx]` has shape (n_actions, n_tilings); sum over the last axis.
sarsa_update: `target = r if terminated else r + gamma * w[a_next, idx_next].sum()` and `delta = target - w[a, idx].sum()`.
Then `w[a, idx] += alpha * delta` and `return delta`. Because each tile index appears once per tiling, the in-place add is safe.

lessons.title: Deep Q-Networks
lessons.summary: Q-learning with a neural network — manual backprop, experience replay, target networks, Huber loss and Double DQN.

exercises.title: A neural network from scratch
hints: forward: `h = x; self._inputs = []; for i in range(self.n_layers): W, b = self.params[2*i], self.params[2*i+1]; self._inputs.append(h); h = h @ W + b` and `np.maximum(h, 0)` if i is not the last layer.
backward: loop `for i in reversed(range(self.n_layers))`. The gradient for W is `self._inputs[i].T @ d`, for b it is `d.sum(axis=0)`.
Before moving to layer i−1: `d = (d @ W.T) * (self._inputs[i] > 0)`. The ReLU that produced layer i's input is exactly where `self._inputs[i] > 0`. Skip this for i = 0.

exercises.title: Replay buffer & Huber loss
hints: add: `i = self.pos; self.obs[i] = s; …; self.pos = (self.pos + 1) % self.capacity; self.size = min(self.size + 1, self.capacity)`.
sample: `idx = self.rng.integers(0, self.size, size=batch_size)` and index every array with the same `idx`.
huber: `a = np.abs(x); np.where(a <= delta, 0.5 * x**2, delta * (a - 0.5 * delta))`. huber_grad: `np.clip(x, -delta, delta)`.

exercises.title: DQN on CartPole
hints: epsilon_by_step: `frac = min(t / decay_steps, 1.0); return start + frac * (end - start)`.

td_targets: plain DQN `next_v = q_next_target.max(axis=1)`; Double DQN `a = q_next_online.argmax(axis=1); next_v = q_next_target[np.arange(len(a)), a]`. Then `rewards + gamma * (1 - terminated) * next_v`.
dqn_loss_and_grad: `rows = np.arange(B); err = q_pred[rows, actions] - targets`; loss is the mean of the Huber of err; `dq = np.zeros_like(q_pred); dq[rows, actions] = np.clip(err, -1, 1) / B`.

lessons.title: Policy Gradients
lessons.summary: Optimise the policy directly — softmax policies, the log-derivative trick, the policy gradient theorem, REINFORCE and baselines.

exercises.title: A softmax policy and its score function
hints: softmax: `z = z - z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True); e = np.exp(z); return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)`.
grad_log_pi: compute `p = policy_probs(theta, x)`, build a one-hot vector for `a`, subtract `p` from it.
`np.outer(x, onehot - p)` has shape (d, n_actions), like theta. sample_action: `int(rng.choice(len(p), p=p))`.

exercises.title: REINFORCE with a baseline on CartPole
hints: Compute `adv = G - X @ w` once, at the start, and use it for the baseline update; normalise a copy for the policy step.
Batch probabilities: `P = softmax(X @ theta)` has shape (N, 2). One-hots: `np.eye(theta.shape[1])[A]`.
`theta += lr * X.T @ ((onehot - P) * adv[:, None]) / N` — that is the mean of Âₜ·outer(xₜ, onehotₜ − πₜ).

lessons.title: Actor-Critic
lessons.summary: A learned critic turns REINFORCE into an online, low-variance learner — advantages, one-step actor-critic, A2C and GAE(λ).

exercises.title: Generalised Advantage Estimation
hints: `next_values = np.append(values[1:], last_value)` lines up V(sₜ₊₁) with each step.
δ = rewards + gamma * (1 - dones) * next_values - values — all vectorised.
GAE: `running = 0; for t in reversed(range(T)): running = delta[t] + gamma * lam * (1 - dones[t]) * running; adv[t] = running`.

exercises.title: Advantage actor-critic on CartPole
hints: actor_loss_grad: `P = softmax(X @ theta)`, `onehot = np.eye(theta.shape[1])[A]`.
`return -X.T @ ((onehot - P) * adv[:, None]) / len(A)`.
critic_loss_grad: `return (v_pred - targets.reshape(-1, 1)) / len(v_pred)`.

lessons.title: Proximal Policy Optimization
lessons.summary: Reuse each batch for several careful updates — probability ratios, the clipped surrogate, value and entropy terms, and why PPO is the default.

exercises.title: The clipped surrogate objective
hints: `ratio = np.exp(logp_new - logp_old)`; `loss = -np.mean(np.minimum(ratio * adv, np.clip(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * adv))`.
`flat = ((adv > 0) & (ratio > 1 + eps)) | ((adv < 0) & (ratio < 1 - eps))` marks samples whose gradient is zero.
`grad = np.where(flat, 0.0, -ratio * adv) / len(adv)`. Diagnostics: `log_r = logp_new - logp_old; r = np.exp(log_r)`.

exercises.title: PPO on CartPole
hints: Normalise: `adv = batch['advantages'][mb]; adv = (adv - adv.mean()) / (adv.std() + 1e-8)`. Rows for fancy indexing: `r = np.arange(len(mb))`, then `logp = np.log(P[r, act] + 1e-12)`.
`_, dlogp = ppo_clip_loss(logp, batch['logp_old'][mb], adv, clip_eps)`; `onehot = np.eye(P.shape[1])[act]`; `dlogits = dlogp[:, None] * (onehot - P) + ent_coef * entropy_loss_grad(P)`.

Critic: `v = critic.forward(obs); target = batch['returns'][mb][:, None] * value_scale; critic_opt.step(critic.backward((v - target) / len(mb)))`. KL: `lr_ = logp - batch['logp_old'][mb]; kls.append(np.mean(np.exp(lr_) - 1 - lr_))`.

lessons.title: Capstone — Core Runner
lessons.summary: Four missions in an original salvage game. Design the state, pick the algorithm, train an agent, and beat par.

exercises.title: Mission 1 · Boot Sequence
hints: The update is Q[s, a] += alpha * (target - Q[s, a]). Only the `terminated` flag removes the bootstrap term.
Tie-breaking: `best = np.flatnonzero(Q[s] == Q[s].max()); return int(rng.choice(best))`. With an all-zero table, plain argmax would always go UP.
epsilon_by_episode: `frac = min(1.0, ep / max(1, decay_frac * episodes)); return eps_start + frac * (eps_end - eps_start)`.

exercises.title: Mission 2 · Vent Maze (1,500-step budget)
hints: Keep `model[(s, a)] = (r, s2, terminated)` and a list of the keys you have seen so you can sample one uniformly with rng.integers(len(keys)).
After each real Q-update, do n_planning updates: pick a random seen (s, a), look up (r, s2, term) and apply the same Q-learning update to it.
eps = max(0.05, 1 - used / (0.5 * budget)) where used = budget - env.steps_left. With n_planning=30 you should reach 47.6.

exercises.title: Mission 3 · Patrol Deck (design the state)
hints: Think of mixed-radix numbers: index = ((cell · n_masks) + mask) · period + phase, with cell = row · W + col and n_masks = 2 ** n_cores.
The cores bitmask: mask = sum(int(got) << i for i, got in enumerate(env.collected)). Phase is env.t % env.period — not env.t itself, or the table would be infinite.
n_states_for(env) = env.h * env.w * 2 ** len(env.core_list) * env.period. The loop body is the same as Mission 1, except s2 = encoder(env) instead of the observation.

exercises.title: Mission 4 · Deep Salvage (DQN)
hints: Double DQN decouples selection from evaluation: a_star = online.forward(S2).argmax(1); q_next = target.forward(S2)[np.arange(len(S2)), a_star].
Only the Q-values of the actions actually taken receive gradient: rows = np.arange(batch); grad = np.zeros_like(qs); grad[rows, A] = huber_grad(qs[rows, A], y).
If training collapses: lower lr (3e-4), longer exploration (explore_frac 0.5), or more total_steps (100k). Watch the replays of failures — getting stuck against walls means it needs more exploration.

lessons.title: Beyond the Training Ground
lessons.summary: Where to go next — real libraries, bigger problems, and the open frontiers of RL.

exercises.title: Open sandbox — bring your own agent
hints: Gymnasium custom envs subclass gymnasium.Env and define observation_space, action_space, reset() and step().
For Core Runner level 4: observation_space = gymnasium.spaces.Box(0, 1, shape=(133,)), action_space = gymnasium.spaces.Discrete(5). Note two of the globals can be negative — use low=-1.
from stable_baselines3 import PPO; model = PPO('MlpPolicy', env).learn(100_000)

lessons.title: Bonus Capstone — Stock the Shelves
lessons.summary: A real-world RL project end to end — retail inventory replenishment, from sales data and a classic planner to an agent judged on a year it has never seen.

exercises.title: Know your demand, then beat a planner
hints: Boolean masks do all the work: `normal = promo == 0`, then `d[normal & (dow == k)].mean()` for each weekday k.
For the lift build `base = np.array([d[normal & (dow == k)].mean() for k in range(7)])`; the expected demand on the promo days is `base[dow[promo == 1]].sum()`.

Python closures capture variables, not values — but evaluate_policy calls your lambda immediately, so `lambda e: s_S_policy(e, s, S)` inside the loop is fine. Keep `best = (None, None, -np.inf)` and update it whenever a profit is larger.

exercises.title: Residual Q-learning: teach the planner new tricks
hints: `_, dow, promo_soon = env.decode_state(obs)`; for the action: `if env.position > s + offset: return 0` else `return env.nearest_action(S + offset - env.position)`.
Head start: `Q[:, int(np.flatnonzero(offsets == 0)[0])] = 1.0`. ε: `eps = max(0.0, eps_start * (1 - ep / (0.7 * episodes)))`.

Inside the episode: `k = int(rng.integers(len(offsets))) if rng.random() < eps else int(np.argmax(Q[c]))`, step with `adjusted_action(env, s, S, offsets[k])`, then `Q[c, k] += alpha * (r + gamma * Q[c2].max() - Q[c, k])` where c2 = context of the new obs. The episode ends when `truncated` is True.

exercises.title: Going real: an out-of-time evaluation
hints: time_split: `{k: v[:n_train] for k, v in history.items()}` and the same with `v[n_train:]`. Lists and numpy arrays both slice this way.

make_envs: `InventoryEnv(demand_series=train['demand'], promo_series=train['promo'], dates=train['dates'], horizon=len(train['demand']), jitter_weeks=2)`; the test env drops jitter and adds `ref_demand=float(np.mean(train['demand']))`.

evaluate: `rows = [summarize(run_policy(env, make_policy(env), seed=s)[1]) for s in seeds]`, then average each key. run_pipeline: `s, S, _, _ = grid_search_sS(train_env)`, `Q, _ = train_residual_q(train_env, s, S, seed=seed)`, and `evaluate(test_env, lambda e: residual_policy(e, Q, s, S))`.
